beats.script_body: The Lower East Side is probably the single most significant multiethnic neighborhood in America. For two hundred years it has been the first area of settlement for migrant and immigrant communities, and it still is. New Yorkers continue to argue about where it begins and ends; the contemporary neighborhood is bordered to the north by Houston Street, to the west by Lafayette, and to the south and east by the East River. But it is better understood as a living multiethnic neighborhood, not one fixed by geographic boundaries.

beats.script_body: Early eighteenth-century maps show this area as the country estates of established Dutch and English settlers — the Stuyvesant, Delancey, Rutgers, DePeyster, and Roosevelt families. After the American Revolution the estates gave way to suburban settlements, and by the mid-nineteenth century the first great influx of immigrants arrived. By the 1840s the largest groups were Irish, Germans, and free blacks. A half century later these had moved northward, replaced by southern and eastern Europeans from Italy, Russia, and Poland. Most of today's immigrant residents are Latino and Asian.

beats.script_body: In 1900 the Lower East Side was the most densely populated spot on earth, with 850 residents per block and nearly 1,000 per acre. A single square block beside Sara Delano Roosevelt Park — bounded by Canal, Hester, Eldridge, and Forsythe Streets — housed 2,628 people in 1890. That same block today houses no residents at all; it holds only a school and a few manufacturers. Other blocks were destroyed to build the approaches to the Manhattan and Williamsburg Bridges in 1903 and 1909, forcing tens of thousands from their homes.

beats.script_body: This green space exists because seven blocks of tenement houses were destroyed between 1932 and 1936. The demolition was part of a Depression-era plan to employ thousands of laborers with federal relief funds: the city proclaimed eminent domain over the tenements, removed the tenants, and tore the buildings down. Like most public spaces in New York, the park is named for a significant New Yorker — Franklin Delano Roosevelt's mother, Sara, who was raised in a manor house, now long gone, on nearby Chrystie Street.

beats.script_body: In 1637 the Bowery was created by New Amsterdam governor Willem Kieft to connect the distant Dutch farms of what we now call the East Village with the city, then south of Wall Street. Some historians claim the name derives from bowerij, the Dutch word for farm; others say it comes from de bowerie, the road to the farms. Either way, it linked the city to the countryside, and by 1776 the Bowery connected New York City all the way to Boston, Massachusetts.

beats.script_body: In the early twentieth century the Bowery was a geographical divider — Little Italy to the west, the Jewish Lower East Side to the east. Between 1878 and 1955 an elevated train ran the length of the street. Before electrification, soot and burning embers falling from the engines made crossing under the tracks dangerous and unpleasant, and the El shrouded the Bowery in darkness, deepening its seedy, dingy atmosphere.

beats.script_body: The Hotel Providence on the southeast corner of Bowery and Grand, at 125 Bowery, is one of eight surviving Bowery flophouses. These private hotels emerged in the early 1870s; the largest, the Mills Hotel, had five hundred rooms and slept over a thousand men. For eight to fifteen dollars a night a male resident gets a four-by-eight-foot cubicle with a cot and a hanging light, sharing toilets and baths on each floor. The rooms are nicknamed cages because the walls do not reach the ceiling — just above the door jamb, the wall is replaced with a wire screen.

beats.script_body: Across the Bowery from the Hotel Providence stood Steve Brodie's Saloon, at 114 Bowery. Brodie, a national champion racewalker, jumped from the Brooklyn Bridge in July 1886, collected a two-hundred-dollar bet for surviving the leap, and used the money to open his saloon here. On the wall behind the bar he painted a large image of himself falling between the bridge and the water. While a regular saloon, Brodie's quickly became a prime tourist spot: for a small consideration he would retell his story to visitors. Should anyone doubt his tale, he would point to the signed affidavit from the nearly dozen witnesses who saw his leap. A cloud of suspicion does remain — those who signed were members of Brodie's gang. For years after his death an old man would pretend to be Brodie and recount the tale, much to the delight of the tourists.

beats.script_body: Wrapped around the old Bowery Bank is the Bowery Savings Bank, built 1894 to 1895 and designed by Stanford White. The L-shaped building's street address is 130 Bowery, and it is one of the few landmarked buildings on the Lower East Side. The Bowery Savings Bank was created in 1834 by three prominent New York businessmen: Hamilton Fish, Peter C. Stuyvesant, and Anson Phelps. The original 1834 safe box is displayed in a small historical exhibit in the restored main banking room.

beats.script_body: Di Palo's Fine Foods, on the northeast corner of Mott and Grand, is one of the few Italian stores left in the midst of New Chinatown. It was opened by Savino Di Palo in 1910 and moved to this corner in 1925, where it has remained ever since. The family comes from Puglia, a rural region known for its dairy farmers and cheese-makers, and the shop still makes its own mozzarella and other cheeses. The low marble counters are reminiscent of the Italian kitchen table — designed for conversation as well as commerce — and the entire front of the store is kept at cheese-curing temperature.

beats.script_body: At 203 Grand Street, on June 22, 1905, Dr. Vincent Sellaro founded the Order of the Sons of Italy in America. Sellaro wanted an organization with a dual mission: to encourage Italian immigrants to work together despite their provincial origins, and to preserve Italian languages and customs in America. The Sons of Italy grew into a national umbrella organization bringing together more than 750 Italian social clubs, family societies, and fraternal orders — much like the Chinese Consolidated Benevolent Association and the Irish Ancient Order of Hibernians.

beats.script_body: Between 1880 and 1920, nearly 4.1 million Italian immigrants came to the United States — no other ethnic group in American history has sent so many in such a short period. Manhattan had fewer than twenty thousand Italian residents in 1880, but by 1930 more than a million New Yorkers were of Italian descent. Most came from the rural south, driven out by extreme poverty, heavy taxation, a population surge, and recurring agricultural crises. Today more than eighty percent of the residents of what used to be Little Italy are Asian; the Italians, like the Irish and Germans before them, have migrated away.

Look inside at the cashiers' cages, still labeled tickets, money exchange, and foreign transfers.

beats.script_body: The Franciscan Fathers who care for the Shrine of San Gennaro, Saint Januarius, keep a rectory at 109 Mulberry Street, with the Church of the Most Precious Blood entered from 113 Baxter Street behind it. San Gennaro, the patron saint of Naples, was martyred by the Romans at Pozzuoli in A.D. 305; the legend says an old couple gathered his blood after his beheading and preserved it in a vial. That blood is said to liquify twice a year — the miracle of San Gennaro — on the first Sunday in May and on September 19. Two thousand years later, in 1917, four Neapolitan businessmen on Mulberry Street decided to celebrate Gennaro's martyrdom, and a great New York tradition was born. beats.script_body: Columbus Park sits atop the former Five Points district and the old Collect Pond. Before 1790 this was a beautiful freshwater pond ringed by low hills and the cottages of wealthy New Yorkers. In 1790 the chief landowner, Sarah Delancey, daughter of colonial governor James Delancey, leased much of it to a consortium of forty-six butchers, who set up a slaughter yard along the shore. Bone-boiling and leather-tanning shops followed, rapidly polluting the pond. The city drained it by way of Canal Street in 1805, leveled the surrounding hills, filled the pond, and renamed the area Paradise Square. But the Collect had been fed by underground springs, and with the constant dampness the ground decayed. The upper-middle-class residents moved out to Greenwich Village and St. John's Park, replaced by poor Irish Catholic immigrants. Paradise Square became Five Points — named for the five-pointed intersection where Park (now Mosco), Worth, and Orange (now Baxter) Streets met, at the southwestern tip of today's Columbus Park.

beats.script_body: Built between 1892 and 1894, Columbus Park was the first open space designed and built for this neighborhood. The person most responsible was Jacob Riis, the Danish American photographer and writer who chronicled the lives of poor New Yorkers. Note how Mulberry Street curves here — this sharp crook is the infamous Mulberry Bend, which residents and newspapers called Ragpickers' Row, Bandits' Roost, and Thieves' Alley.

beats.script_body: On the south corner of Mosco and Mulberry, at 28 Mulberry, a building with marble pillars and a terra-cotta eagle was Antonio Cuneo's 1881 bank. Cuneo, a Piedmontese immigrant who arrived in 1855, began selling nuts and fruit from a pushcart and slowly built a real estate and banking empire. In 1887 a U.S. congressional investigation found the bank operated under the padrone system — a labor arrangement in which the bank, for a fee, ran an agency in Naples coordinating prepaid steamer tickets and requests for underpaid labor. The system, outlawed in 1885 by the Contract Labor Law, brought immigrants in to undercut American wages.

beats.script_body: At the southern end of the block, where Mulberry meets Worth, was the Cow Bay section of Five Points — the largest free-black neighborhood in Manhattan in the early nineteenth century. In 1805, nearly 1,200 of the 1,960 free blacks in Manhattan lived in this general area, and by 1825 the community had built seven churches. beats.script_body: The parish was founded in 1827 by Padre Félix Varela, New York's first Spanish-speaking priest. Born in Havana in 1788, Varela was an outspoken voice for Cuban independence; after his expulsion from Cuba he became a leader of this church and its Irish parishioners. The plaque calls him Father to needy Irish immigrants. By the early 1880s the Irish began migrating out and Italians used the basement for services — the two congregations worshiped the same God but in styles different enough that they didn't worship together. In 1902 an Italian priest, Father Cappo, moved the Italian community upstairs to sit with the Irish, and this became the church of Enrico Caruso, Jimmy Durante, and Mother Cabrini, the first naturalized American saint. By the 1960s the congregation had become increasingly Chinese; today it is almost exclusively so, with Mass given in Cantonese, Mandarin, and English.

beats.script_body: Of all the immigrant groups that passed through the Lower East Side, the Chinese have had the longest continuous presence — a small group of sailors lived here as early as 1850, and by 1859 the New York Times estimated some 150 Chinese in the district. After the transcontinental railroad's completion in 1869 and rising anti-Chinese nativism, Chinese immigrants moved to cities, and Mott, Pell, and Doyers Streets became home to two thousand Chinese within a decade. America's anti-Chinese bigotry culminated in the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 — the Chinese became the first and only ethnic group excluded from admission and denied citizenship. Because the laborers already here could not bring their wives, the result was a bachelor society: in 1910 the New York ratio of Chinese young men to young women aged fifteen to twenty-one was 3,961 to 100. The act was finally revoked in 1943, and after the Immigration Act of 1965 the neighborhood's Chinese population exploded from 11,000 in 1960 to nearly 150,000 by 1995.

beats.script_body: At No. 24 Pell Street stands the former Sun Wui Association, the last wooden pagoda building in Chinatown and a great example of symbolism in Chinatown architecture. The roof is a pagoda topped with two fish — symbols of good luck and abundance, since the word for fish in many Chinese languages sounds like the one for profit or surplus. Its colors are red, gold, and green: red for good luck, gold for money or wealth, green for growth and flowering. Many signs in Chinatown combine these three traditional colors.

Buried here are Jewish American soldiers who fought in the American Revolution and Benjamin Mendes-Seixas, one of the founders of the New York Stock Exchange. When the cemetery was established it lay over a mile north of the city limits; Dutch governor Peter Stuyvesant, New York's first prominent anti-Semite, ordered it built outside New Amsterdam proper. The congregation still exists, meeting at Seventieth Street and Central Park West.

beats.script_body: The Irish are one of the oldest immigrant groups in New York; the first St. Patrick's Day parade was held in 1766, and in 1784 the Society of the Friendly Sons of St. Patrick became the city's first specifically ethnic self-help organization. Mass Irish immigration began in the 1820s and peaked in the famine years of 1845 to 1855; by 1860 roughly one in six city residents claimed Irish heritage. The Irish helped found the police and fire departments and, through Tammany Hall, came to dominate Democratic politics by the 1870s. Tammany was a rampantly corrupt machine, but to immigrant Irish it was a crucial institution offering social welfare in exchange for a vote — and it was behind the 1880 election of William Grace, New York's first Irish Catholic mayor.

beats.script_body: The 1976 elementary school P.S. 124 on Division Street, opposite Market Street, is named for Yung Wing — both school and man serving as role models for the area's Chinese immigrant children. Yung Wing, born near Macao in 1828, came to the United States as a student in 1847, entered Yale, and in 1854 became the first Chinese person to graduate from an American college. He devoted his life to the modernization of China and served as a Chinese diplomat in the United States, remaining in America until his death.

beats.script_body: The Manhattan Bridge, the third bridge connecting Lower Manhattan with Brooklyn, was designed by engineer Gustav Lindenthal in 1905 and was the divider between Chinatown and the old Jewish East Side. The structure is greatly enhanced by its restored 1916 colonnade at the Canal Street entrance. Built by the architects Carrère & Hastings, this triumphal arch is a wonderful example of the City Beautiful movement, which from 1890 to World War I saw New York invest in beautifying its neighborhoods — planting trees, clearing slums for parks, and adding architectural enhancements.

beats.script_body: The East European Jews began arriving in large numbers in the early 1880s and settled almost exclusively in the Lower East Side, regrouping not as Jews but by country and region — Russians, Poles, and Hungarians forming distinct enclaves. Because American law forbids asking an immigrant's religion, estimates of how many Jews came range widely, from three to five million. Unlike most Italians, most Jews were fleeing political or religious oppression and came to stay: for every thousand Jews who arrived through Ellis Island, only three chose to return to Europe. The population of the Lower East Side climaxed at some 542,000 residents in 1910, then declined as subways opened newer neighborhoods uptown and in the outer boroughs.

beats.script_body: At 12-16 Eldridge Street stands the Congregation Khal Adath Jeshurun and Anshe Lubz Synagogue, popularly the Eldridge Street Synagogue. Built in 1886-87 by the Herter brothers, German architects, in a Moorish revival and Romanesque style, it was named a National Historic Landmark in 1996. The exterior rose window resembles those of Christian churches but is distinctly Jewish: it contains twelve rondels, smaller windows representing the twelve tribes of Israel. Note too the recurring patterns — two tablets for the Ten Commandments, five windows for the five books of the Torah, and three sets of stairs leading to four sets of doors for the Jewish biblical matriarchs and patriarchs. The interior is a beautiful Orthodox synagogue with women's balconies, designed in Moorish and Sephardic style.

beats.script_body: The wide Allen Street thoroughfare is very different today than in the heyday of the Jewish Lower East Side. Before 1932 the street was only thirty-two feet wide and completely covered by an elevated train; that year the buildings on the east side were torn down and the street widened to 138 feet for the automobile. The city removed the El in 1942, planning a Second Avenue subway to connect the northern Bronx with Wall Street. Construction finally began in 1972 but was soon discontinued for lack of money — New York, like so many American cities, became beholden to the automobile at the expense of public transit.

beats.script_body: On the southwest corner of Canal and Orchard stands the tall former Jarmulovsky Bank, a story of how one could make it and lose it on the Lower East Side. Sender Jarmulovsky began his banking career with savings from his peddler days and built this building in homage to himself in 1912. The bank catered to poor immigrants, especially those sending money back to family in the Old World. Jarmulovsky died a few months after the building was finished, and his sons continued the business. Then came World War I: Jewish depositors rushed to withdraw their money to help family in Europe, and, distrusting paper money, demanded silver and gold coins. The runs forced the state to close the bank on August 4, 1914. The New York Times reported that two thousand people demonstrated in front of the bank, a mob of fifteen hundred enraged depositors required a hundred policemen to restrain, and five hundred people gathered outside Jarmulovsky's apartment, forcing the family to flee.

beats.script_body: Four buildings at 27-33 Orchard Street are excellent examples of pre-law tenements — multifamily dwellings built before 1879, among the oldest and least desirable housing in New York City. Each building holds sixteen apartments, four to a floor. Each apartment averages three rooms totaling 270 square feet: a kitchen, bedroom, and living room, each only nine by ten feet. The only windows are two in the living room; there is no elevator, and before 1901 no indoor plumbing — residents shared backyard outhouses, cleaned out twice a year, and hand pumps. Compare these with the more ornate tenements nearby: a few doors back, at 14-16 Orchard, the terra-cotta details show two rows of Jewish stars surrounded by twelve pomegranates. Contrary to popular lore these were never Jewish buildings — the decoration was meant to entice Jews to live here.

beats.script_body: Hester Street between Orchard and Essex was the site of the Khazzer Mark — Pig Market in Yiddish — where Jewish and Italian peddlers set up pushcarts to sell an incredible array of goods. Why Pig Market? Jacob Riis described turn-of-the-century Hester Street as a place where scarcely anything other than pork could not be hawked from a wagon, at ridiculously low prices, amid crowds pushing, struggling, babbling, and shouting in foreign tongues — a veritable Babel of confusion. Pushcart peddling was finally abolished by Mayor Fiorello La Guardia in 1935, who built enclosed markets and offered peddlers heated, policed buildings in exchange for a license and taxes.

beats.script_body: The small three-acre Seward Park, built in 1901 and named for Lincoln's secretary of state William Seward, was the first park built in this part of the neighborhood. The city tore down three blocks of tenement houses and displaced nearly three thousand people to create it — like Columbus Park, less a philanthropic gift than an early attempt at slum clearance and population control. The park is best known as a gathering point for striking garment workers: in 1909, 1912, and 1916, thousands of workers gathered here and gazed south toward the Jewish Daily Forward Building, waiting for reports on their demands for a living wage and an eight-hour day.

beats.script_body: Look southeast across the square at the old Forverts Building at 173 East Broadway. Built in 1912 and designed by George A. Boehm, the twelve-story Jewish Daily Forward Building was a towering presence over the neighborhood, with the name Forverts inscribed across the top beneath a huge clock. From 1901 until 1951 the Forward was edited by Abraham Cahan, a Russian Jewish immigrant who made it the most widely read Yiddish paper in the world and used it as an Americanizing tool to introduce East European Jews to American life. The most popular section was the Bintel Brief, the Bundle of Letters, where readers presented their problems and received answers from the editors. The Forward moved out in 1975; the building became an evangelical Protestant church, and in 1999 it was sold to a developer transforming it into luxury condominiums — the first luxury doorman condo in the Lower East Side, a clear sign of the gentrification to come.

beats.script_body: At the southeast corner of East Broadway and Jefferson is the Educational Alliance, known as the Edgies. Built in 1889 by uptown German Jews to Americanize the East European immigrants, it offered day and evening classes in English, citizenship, and hygiene, coordinated the immigration process for Jews arriving at Ellis Island, and became the center for American relief to Jews in Nazi-occupied Europe. The main building was renamed for David Sarnoff after a 1960s renovation. Sarnoff's life is a veritable Horatio Alger story: born in Russia in 1891, he arrived in America at age nine, and the family's first home was a fourth-floor walk-up on Monroe Street at ten dollars a month. Within days he was earning money selling the Yiddish paper Tageblatt at four a.m. At night he took English classes here at the Educational Alliance. From newsboy to messenger at the Commercial Cable Company, his career took off — he eventually became president and CEO of RCA and was instrumental in RCA's creation of NBC television in 1926.

beats.script_body: The converted double tenement at 229 East Broadway was the first home of the Hebrew Sheltering and Immigrant Aid Society, now known as HIAS. Note how the communities are organized by landslayt, or homeland, rather than by religious denomination.

beats.script_body: St. Mary's Church, on the corner of Grand and Ridge Streets, is the oldest Catholic church building in all of New York City and its third parish, founded in 1827. Originally built in 1833, its brick facade and double spires were added in 1871 by architect Patrick C. Keely. Unlike other Lower East Side houses of worship, this building has served the Catholic community without interruption since it was erected — no other house of worship has served one religion for so long in this neighborhood. When the Catholic Church abolished the mandatory Latin Mass in 1965, churches like this became more diverse; St. Mary's now offers Mass in English and Spanish.

beats.script_body: On the north side of Grand between Clinton and Suffolk, no. 402 is a wonderful 1830s merchant house, shop at street level and family above. Next to it stands a fine example of a dumbbell tenement. The tenement law changed in 1887, and the crucial addition was the airshaft, along with a required window in every room. But the airshafts failed in their mission to provide fresh air — they mostly cost residents usable square footage. An 1888 journal described them as great prison-like structures of brick, with a narrow court-yard that was a damp, foul-smelling place supposed to do duty as an airshaft, and that in case of fire would be perfect death-traps.

beats.script_body: At 60 Norfolk is the Beth Hamedrash Hagadol, the Great House of Study. Built in 1850 as the Norfolk Baptist Church and purchased by a Jewish congregation in 1885, it is the oldest Russian Ashkenazic Orthodox congregation in the United States, formed in 1852. In 1888 it became the pulpit of Rabbi Jacob Joseph, the first and only chief rabbi of New York's Orthodox community — but the neighborhood's diverse Jewish communities proved unable to sustain a single chief rabbi. Once the largest Russian synagogue in the country, the congregation is now small; the building is worth visiting for its beautiful Gothic interior and was made a New York Historical Landmark in January 1967.

beats.script_body: Broome Street is worth pondering for a moment. In 1946 Robert Moses, the great builder and destroyer of New York, wanted to run the Lower Manhattan Expressway across it, connecting the Holland Tunnel with the Williamsburg and Manhattan Bridges. It would have stood about a hundred feet above the ground and devastated this neighborhood. Luckily, Moses was foiled.

beats.script_body: Note the very small plaque on the wall at what would be 60 Essex Street. This was the site of Sinsheimer's Cafe, where on October 13, 1843, the B'nai Brith — Sons of the Covenant — was organized by immigrant German Jews. Like the other immigrant groups' organizations, it was founded as a self-help and defensive society to protect American Jews against anti-immigrant sentiment, and it is the oldest Jewish fraternal organization in America.
